kits.familyName: An email that might be a scam
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. An email arrives that appears to come from {lead|the}, asking you to handle something right away.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you get an email that looks like it is from {lead|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says these warnings are overblown and to just get it done.
You are in the middle of a busy afternoon.
detail: The email has the workplace logo at the top.

tiers.1: Handing over a password can expose every system you can reach.
tiers.2: Confirming who sent a message comes before acting on it.
tiers.3: An unexpected attachment stays closed until the sender is confirmed.
tiers.4: Spreading a suspicious email puts more people at risk.

fact: The email asks you to confirm your password through a link, and the security policy says never to do that.
issues.action: Leave the link alone and report the email the way the security policy describes.
issues.brief: skip the link and report the email
issues.reason: Password requests through email links are a common scam. Reporting it protects you and warns the security team.
issues.lesson: Never enter your password through a link in an unexpected email; report it instead.

shortcut.text: Click the link just to see whether the page looks real.
shortcut.brief: click to see if it looks real
shortcut.why: Fake login pages are designed to look real, and clicking can itself cause harm.
shortcut.mis: You can spot a fake page by looking at it.

fact: The sender's address is spelled slightly differently from {lead|the}'s usual address.
clear: You called {lead|the} at the usual number, and {lead|the} confirmed sending the email.
issues.done: the sender was already confirmed by phone
issues.action: Check with {lead|the} by phone or in person, not by replying, before doing anything.
issues.reason: A lookalike address is a warning sign. Replying goes to the scammer, so confirm another way.
issues.lesson: Confirm a suspicious message's sender through a separate, known channel.

shortcut.text: Reply to the email and ask whether it is really from {lead|the}.
shortcut.brief: reply and ask if it is real
shortcut.why: A reply goes straight to whoever sent it, who will simply say yes.
shortcut.mis: Replying is a good way to verify a sender.

fact: The email includes an attachment called "invoice" that you were not expecting.
issues.action: Leave the attachment unopened until the sender is confirmed.
issues.reason: Unexpected attachments are a common way to deliver harmful software.
issues.lesson: Do not open unexpected attachments until you confirm who sent them.

shortcut.text: Open the attachment, since invoices are normal at work.
shortcut.brief: open it since invoices are normal
shortcut.why: An invoice you were not expecting is exactly the kind of file scammers use.

fact: {coworker} suggests forwarding the email to the whole team to ask if anyone thinks it is real.
issues.short: the idea of forwarding it to everyone
issues.action: Report the email through the security process instead of forwarding it.
issues.reason: Forwarding spreads the risk to everyone who receives it. The security team is the right audience.
issues.lesson: Report suspicious messages to security rather than spreading them.

shortcut.text: Forward it to the team so everyone can vote on it.
shortcut.why: Forwarding gives every coworker a chance to click the harmful link.
shortcut.mis: Sharing a threat helps everyone stay safe.

proceed.text: Go ahead with the request in the email.
proceed.why: The sender is confirmed and nothing in the email raises a warning, so the request can be handled.
proceed.lesson: Act on requests once you have confirmed they are real.

generic.text: Delete the email and say nothing to anyone.
generic.why: Deleting without reporting leaves others exposed to the same scam.
generic.mis: Deleting a scam is the same as reporting it.

generic.text: Turn off your computer and leave it off for the day.
generic.why: Turning off your computer does not deal with the email or warn anyone.

overcaution.text: Refuse to handle any email from {lead|the} for the rest of the week.
overcaution.why: The sender is confirmed. Refusing real requests stops your work for no reason.

setup: An unexpected email at {workplace|the} asks you to take action quickly.

sender: The sender's address looks almost, but not exactly, right.
attachment: The email has an attachment you did not expect.

steps.text: Report it through the security process
Delete it once it has been reported

rel: Pausing is what keeps the file closed.
Your report should include what you learned.
The report covers the unopened file.
Security may need the email, so report first.
process.lesson: Pause, verify through a known channel, report, and only then delete.

review.notes: Security policy stated in the password fact. General phishing guidance, no legal claims.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, where your computer gives you access to {private}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you handle {private} on the computer at your station.
detail: Your station is near the front.

fact: You need to step away, and {private} are open on your screen where others could see.
issues.short: the information open on your screen
issues.action: Lock your screen before you step away.
issues.reason: Anyone walking by could see confidential information. Locking takes a second and protects it.
issues.lesson: Lock your screen whenever you step away.

shortcut.text: Turn the monitor slightly away and step out quickly.
shortcut.why: Angling the screen does not stop someone from seeing or using it.
shortcut.mis: Partly hiding a screen is enough.

fact: You realize you just emailed a file with {private} to the wrong person.
issues.short: the email sent to the wrong person
issues.action: Tell {lead|the} right away so the mistake can be handled quickly.
issues.reason: Quick reporting gives the workplace the best chance to limit the harm, such as asking for the email to be deleted.
issues.lesson: Report security mistakes immediately, even your own.

shortcut.text: Say nothing and hope the person deletes it.
shortcut.why: Hiding the mistake removes the chance to limit the damage.
shortcut.mis: Small security mistakes are best kept quiet.

fact: {coworker} asks to use your login because theirs is locked, and the policy says logins are never shared.
issues.short: the request to share your login
issues.action: Decline, and suggest {coworker} contact the help desk to unlock the account.
issues.reason: Shared logins break the policy and make it impossible to know who did what.
issues.lesson: Never share your login, even with a trusted coworker.

shortcut.text: Log in for {coworker} and stay nearby while they work.
shortcut.why: Logging in for someone is still sharing access, which the policy forbids.
shortcut.mis: Sharing is fine if you watch what they do.

fact: You find an unlabeled USB drive in the parking lot.
issues.action: Hand the drive to {lead|the} or the help desk without plugging it in.
issues.reason: Unknown drives can carry harmful software. Handing it in lets the right people deal with it safely.
issues.lesson: Never plug in devices you find; hand them in.

shortcut.text: Plug it in to see whose it is so you can return it.
shortcut.why: Plugging in an unknown drive can install harmful software.
shortcut.mis: Plugging in a drive is harmless.

fact: You want to download a game on the work computer during break, which the acceptable-use policy forbids.
issues.action: Skip the download, since the acceptable-use policy does not allow it.
issues.reason: Acceptable-use rules exist because downloads can bring in harmful software and use work resources.
issues.lesson: Follow acceptable-use rules on work devices, even on your break.

shortcut.text: Download it, since it is your break and not work time.
shortcut.why: The policy applies to the work computer at all times.
shortcut.mis: Work rules do not apply during breaks.

proceed.text: Carry on with your work, since none of this is a real risk.
proceed.why: Each of these situations is a real security risk that needs a response.
proceed.lesson: Small security habits protect confidential information every day.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} what they usually do and copy that.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the policy, and it may be unsafe.
generic.mis: Common practice is always safe practice.

generic.text: Write your password on a note under the keyboard to save time later.
generic.why: Written passwords near a computer are easy for others to find.
generic.mis: Hidden notes are a safe place for passwords.

title: Workstation security reminders
intro: You are checking this reminder sheet before it is posted at every station.
doc.lesson: Security reminders must protect logins, devices and confidential information.

lines.text: Lock your screen every time you leave your station.
lines.fine: Protects information when you are away.

lines.text: Never share your login; the help desk can unlock accounts.
lines.fine: Keeps each login tied to one person.

bad.text: Share your login with trusted coworkers when theirs is locked.
bad.why: Sharing logins breaks security and accountability, no matter how trusted the person is.

lines.text: Hand in any device you find; never plug it in.

bad.text: Plug in found USB drives to identify the owner.
bad.why: Unknown drives can carry malware. They should be handed in, not plugged in.

lines.text: Report suspicious emails to the help desk.
lines.fine: Routes threats to the right team.

lines.text: If you send confidential information to the wrong person, tell {lead|the} right away.

bad.text: If you send confidential information to the wrong person, wait to see if they notice.
bad.why: Waiting removes the chance to limit the harm. Mistakes should be reported immediately.

lines.text: Use a long passphrase and keep it to yourself.

bad.text: Write your password on a sticky note so you do not forget it.
bad.why: Written passwords are easy for others to find and use.

review.notes: Login-sharing and acceptable-use rules stated as policy. Beginner-only issues because these would not naturally co-occur.

setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. A caller says they work for a partner company and asks you to send them {private}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you get a phone request to send {private} to someone outside the team.
pressure: The caller says their boss needs it within the hour.
{coworker3} says it is easier to just send it.
detail: The call came in on the main line.

tiers.1: Identity must be confirmed before confidential information goes anywhere.
tiers.2: Only the person the policy names can approve sharing.
tiers.3: Share only the information that is actually needed.
tiers.4: The sending method has to protect the information.
tiers.5: Keeping a record of what was shared comes last.

fact: You have never heard of the caller, and the policy says outside requests must be verified first.
clear: You called the partner company's listed number, and they confirmed the caller works there.
issues.action: Verify the caller through the company's listed number before sharing anything.
issues.reason: Scammers often pose as partners. Checking through a number you find yourself confirms who is asking.
issues.lesson: Verify who is asking before sharing confidential information.

shortcut.text: Trust the caller, since they know details about the account.
shortcut.why: Scammers often know a few details. That is not verification.
shortcut.mis: Knowing details proves who someone is.

fact: The policy says {lead|the} must approve any sharing of {private} outside the team.
clear: {Lead|the} already approved sharing these records with this partner.
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} to approve the request before sending anything.
issues.reason: The policy puts this decision with the lead, who knows whether the partner should receive the records.
issues.lesson: Follow the approval steps before sharing protected information.

shortcut.text: Send it, since partners usually get this kind of information.
shortcut.brief: send it because partners usually do
shortcut.why: Usual practice is not approval. The policy requires the lead's approval.

fact: The caller asks for the full file, but the request only needs two items from it.
issues.short: the request for more than is needed
issues.action: Offer to share only the two items the request actually needs.
issues.reason: Sharing only what is needed limits the harm if the information is lost or misused.
issues.lesson: Share the minimum information needed for the task.

shortcut.text: Send the full file so they do not have to ask again.
shortcut.why: Extra information adds risk without any benefit.

fact: The caller asks you to text the information to a personal phone.
clear: The partner has an approved secure portal set up for these files.
issues.done: a secure portal is already set up
issues.action: Send it only through the approved secure method, not by text.
issues.reason: Text messages to personal phones are not protected. Approved channels keep the information secure.
issues.lesson: Send confidential information only through approved, secure channels.

shortcut.text: Text it, since it is faster and the caller asked.
shortcut.why: Speed does not make an unprotected channel safe.
shortcut.mis: The requester decides how information is sent.

fact: The policy says every outside sharing must be noted in {record|the}.
issues.action: Note in {record|the} what you shared, with whom and when.
issues.reason: A sharing record lets the workplace track where confidential information has gone.
issues.lesson: Record what confidential information you share and with whom.

shortcut.text: Skip the note, since the email shows what was sent.
shortcut.why: The policy requires the record, and emails are not always kept or searchable.

proceed.text: Send the requested information through the usual approved method.
proceed.why: The requester is verified, sharing is approved and the method is secure, so the request can be completed.
proceed.lesson: Share protected information only after verification, approval and a secure method are in place.

generic.text: Put the caller on hold and hope they hang up.
generic.why: Avoiding the request does not resolve it and is unprofessional.
generic.mis: Ignoring a hard request makes it go away.

generic.text: Read the information aloud over the phone to save time.
generic.why: Reading confidential information aloud bypasses every check the policy requires.
generic.mis: Saying something aloud is safer than sending it.

overcaution.text: Refuse the request and tell the caller never to call again.
overcaution.why: The request is verified and approved; refusing blocks legitimate work.
overcaution.mis: Every outside request is a threat.

setup: A partner company has asked {workplace|the} for {private}.

identity: You do not recognize the person asking.
log: The policy requires a record of every outside sharing.

steps.text: Call back on the company's listed number
Pick out only the items needed
Send them through the secure method

rel: The lead needs to know who is really asking.
Nothing is sent before the requester is verified.
Choose what to send before sending.
You record what was actually sent.
process.lesson: Verify, approve, limit, send securely, then record.

title: Your reply to the partner company
intro: You are about to reply to the partner company's request. Check the message first.
doc.lesson: Replies about confidential information must follow verification, approval, minimum sharing and secure delivery.

lines.text: We confirmed your request through your company's main number.
Attached through our secure portal are the two items you need.

bad.text: I attached the full file of {private} in case it helps.
bad.why: Sending the whole file shares far more than needed.

lines.text: Please download them from the portal within 7 days.
lines.fine: Secure delivery with a time limit.

bad.text: I will also text the same files to your personal phone.
bad.why: Personal phones and texts are not approved, secure channels.

lines.text: Let me know if you have trouble with the portal.

bad.text: Feel free to forward them to anyone on your team.
bad.why: The approval covered this requester; inviting wider forwarding defeats the limits.

review.notes: Verification, approval and logging stated as workplace policy.
